sections.title: Name and recognition
sections.text: Boletus reticulatus Schaeff. is the name accepted by Species Fungorum; B. aestivalis (Paulet) Fr. is treated as a synonym. The cap, commonly 5–20 cm across, is hemispherical at first, then convex to nearly flat, hazelnut to ochre-brown, matte and finely velvety. It may crack into patches in dry weather, exposing the pale flesh. The tubes and pores are white at first, then cream, yellow to yellow-green or olive at maturity; they generally do not blue when pressed. The stem is bulbous when young, later club-shaped or cylindrical, pale brown, with a raised net pattern often pronounced on the upper half and paler than the background. The flesh is white and does not change when cut; it softens in older specimens. The spore print is olive-brown.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: This ectomycorrhizal bolete grows in broadleaf and mixed woodland, especially with oaks, and also with beech and lime; occasional records under conifers also exist. Records vary by region. It fruits from late spring into autumn, including after warm, damp periods; May–November is documented in central Europe, not a universal calendar.

sections.title: Similar species and caution
sections.text: The penny bun (Boletus edulis) shares white flesh and pores, but its cap often has a paler margin and its stem reticulation is usually less extensive. The bitter bolete (Tylopilus felleus) can also have a netted stem; its pores become pinkish and its flesh is very bitter. No single feature, and no image on this page, can securely identify a collected specimen. The DGfM and VAPKO include B. reticulatus on their recommended edible mushroom lists; those lists do not verify a photo identification or a particular find.

traits: Hazelnut-brown cap, matte and velvety when young, often cracking into patches in dry weather
Tubes white, then cream, yellow to yellow-green or olive; pores generally do not blue
Stem bulbous, then club-shaped or cylindrical, with a raised pale net pattern
White flesh, unchanged when cut; olive-brown spore print
Broadleaf woodland, especially with oak, also beech and lime; late spring to autumn
safetyNote: The DGfM and VAPKO list Boletus reticulatus among recommended edible mushrooms. This does not confirm the identity of a collection, and a picture is not enough to decide whether to eat a specimen. Do not consume an uncertain mushroom; have it checked by a qualified mycologist or mushroom controller.
